Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2605.17254v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Property prediction and inverse structural design of catalytic materials are typically modeled as two independent tasks: the former predicts target properties from given structures, whereas the latter generates candidate structures conditioned on desired properties. Although this decoupled paradigm facilitates the construction of a ``generation--evaluation--screening'' workflow, the two models may have different domains of applicability because they are trained on different data distributions. Consequently, during closed-loop optimization, the generative model may produce structures that fall outside the reliable applicability domain of the evaluation model, while prediction errors from the evaluator may accumulate over successive iterations, ultimately degrading inverse-design performance. In this work, we propose CatalyticMLLM, a unified graph--text multimodal large language model for catalytic materials that integrates \textbf{property prediction} and \textbf{inverse design} within a single model and a shared representation space. Under this unified framework, CatalyticMLLM not only performs reliable property prediction by jointly leveraging three-dimensional structures and textual information, but also generates and screens physically feasible CIF candidates conditioned on target properties, thereby establishing a closed-loop workflow of ``inverse design--prediction--screening--redesign.'' Experimental results demonstrate that the unified paradigm outperforms decoupled baselines in both catalytic relaxation-energy prediction and inverse-design tasks, validating the effectiveness of jointly modeling property prediction and structure generation within a single multimodal model.

On the one hand, this allows one to introduce domain knowledge that can speed up the search for a solution through the method library. On the other hand, it creates challenges that go beyond those of classical state-space search. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can generate effective search heuristics for HTN planning, extending the methodology of Corr\^ea et al. (arXiv:2503.18809) from classical to hierarchical planning. Using the Pytrich planner on seven standard total-order HTN benchmark domains, we evaluate heuristics generated by nine LLMs under domain-specific prompting and compare them against two established domain-independent heuristics in the same planner and against the PANDA planner. A configuration fixed in advance solves more instances than either domain-independent heuristic, the best generated heuristics expand fewer nodes than both on most instances, and the virtual best over all models is on par with PANDA in coverage.

To address this challenge, we propose ScrapMem, a bio-inspired framework that consolidates each day's heterogeneous records into a unified "Scrapbook Page." ScrapMem introduces Optical Forgetting, an optical compression mechanism that progressively reduces the resolution and JPEG quality of older pages, lowering storage costs while keeping recent evidence at higher fidelity. To preserve semantic consistency and support structured retrieval, we construct an Episodic Memory Graph (EM-Graph) that organizes semantic nodes into causal-temporal EM-Paths. This design separates a stable retrieval structure from aging visual evidence, allowing relevant episodes to remain accessible as page fidelity decreases. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in recent times, the AI community has witnessed a remarkable surge in the development of larger and more performant language models, such as Falcon 40B, LLaMa-2 70B, Falcon 40B, MPT 30B, and in the imaging domain with models like SD2.1 and SDXL.

  • Our new compressed models have been trained on Knowledge-Distillation (KD) techniques and the work has been largely based on this paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in recent times, the AI community has witnessed a remarkable surge in the development of larger and more performant language models, such as Falcon 40B, LLaMa-2 70B, Falcon 40B, MPT 30B, and in the imaging domain with models like SD2.1 and SDXL. These advancements have undoubtedly pushed the boundaries of what AI can achieve, enabling highly versatile and state-of-the-art image generation and language understanding capabilities. However, as we marvel at the power and complexity of these models, it is essential to recognize a growing need to make AI models smaller, efficient, and more accessible, particularly by open-sourcing them.

It has been revealed that at Segmind, we have been working on how to make generative AI models faster and cheaper. Last year, we have open-sourced our accelerated SD-WebUI library called voltaML, which is a AITemplate/TensorRT based inference acceleration library that has delivered between 4-6X increase in the inference speed. To continue towards the goal of making generative models faster, smaller and cheaper, we are open-sourcing the weights and training code of our compressed SD models; SD-Small and SD-Tiny. The pretrained checkpoints are available on Huggingface 🤗.

Our new compressed models have been trained on Knowledge-Distillation (KD) techniques and the work has been largely based on this paper. The authors describe a Block-removal Knowledge-Distillation method where some of the UNet layers are removed and the student model weights are trained. Using the KD methods described in the paper, we were able to train two compressed models using the 🧨 diffusers library; Small and Tiny, that have 35% and 55% fewer parameters, respectively than the base model while achieving comparable image fidelity as the base model. We have open-sourced our distillation code in this repo and pretrained checkpoints on Huggingface 🤗.

In a recent development, knowledge-Distillation training a neural network is similar to a teacher guiding a student step-by-step. A large teacher model is pre-trained on a large amount of data and then a smaller model is trained on a smaller dataset, to imitate the outputs of the larger model along with classical training on the dataset.

In this particular type of knowledge distillation, the student model is trained to do the normal diffusion task of recovering an image from pure noise, but at the same time, the model is made to match the output of the larger teacher model. The matching of outputs happens at every block of the U-nets, hence the model quality is mostly preserved. So, using the previous analogy, we can say that during this kind of distillation, the student will not only try to learn from the Questions and Answers but also from the Teacher’s answers, as well as the step by step method of getting to the answer. We have 3 components in the loss function to achieve this, firstly the traditional loss between latents of the target image and latents of the generated image. Secondly, the loss between latents of the image generated by the teacher and latents of image generated by the student. And lastly, and the most notable component, is the feature level loss, which is the loss between the outputs of each of the blocks of the teacher and the student.

Industry observers note that combining all of this makes up the Knowledge-Distillation training. Below is an architecture of the Block Removed UNet used in the KD as described in the paper.

Sources indicate that image taken from the paper “On Architectural Compression of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models” by Shinkook. et. al.

According to recent reports, we have taken Realistic-Vision 4.0 as our base teacher model and have trained on the LAION Art Aesthetic dataset with image scores above 7.5, because of their high quality image descriptions. Unlike the paper, we have chosen to train the two models on 1M images for 100K steps for the Small and 125K steps for the Tiny mode respectively. The code for the distillation training can be found here.

The Model can be used using the DiffusionPipeline from 🧨 diffusers.

We have observed that distilled models are up to 100% faster than the original base models. The Benchmarking code can be found here.

Sources indicate that the distilled models are in early phase and the outputs may not be at a production quality yet. These models may not be the best general models. They are best used as fine-tuned or LoRA trained on specific concepts/styles. Distilled models are not very good at composibility or multiconcepts yet.

Industry observers note that we have fine-tuned our sd-tiny model on portrait images generated with the Realistic Vision v4.0 model. Below are the fine tuning parameters used.

We were able to produce image quality close to the images produced by the original model, with almost 40% fewer parameters and the sample results below speak for themselves:.

The code for fine-tuning the base models can be found here.

One of the advantages of LoRA training on a distilled model is faster training. Below are some of the images of the first LoRA we trained on the distilled model on some abstract concepts. The code for the LoRA training can be found here.

In a recent development, arXiv:2603.27910v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI agents that talk with people across many sessions need long-term memory to stay coherent and personalized. Existing approaches use either flat retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that ignores how memories connect, or entity-centric knowledge graphs. Entity-centric graphs split each message into separate triples, which loses its context, and in conversations the speakers become hubs linked to almost every message, so propagation through them tells retrieval little. We present GAAMA, a graph-augmented associative memory that organizes conversations around topics. It keeps verbatim episodes, uses an LLM to distill them into atomic facts and topic concepts, and then synthesizes higher-order reflections. These four node types are linked by five kinds of structural edges, and topic concepts supply the cross-cutting paths, so mega-hubs do not form. Retrieval blends nearest-neighbor similarity search with Personalized PageRank whose transitions depend on edge type. We also introduce GRAFT (Graph Repair by Augmenting Facts & Topology), an offline repair step: for questions whose retrieved evidence fell short, a bounded ReAct agent searches memory again and records the grounded answer as a fresh fact, so later questions find it directly without extra query-time cost. On LoCoMo10, GAAMA achieves the highest average score of all compared methods (79.1%) and is competitive in every question category; GRAFT adds a small further gain. In a controlled comparison, replacing GAAMA's concept-linked facts with entity relation triples lowers reward by 3.0 pp. On MemoryArena, scored on what memory alone determines, GAAMA has the best score on average.

VeRA: Verified Reasoning Data Augmentation at Scale

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (281 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2602.13217v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Static benchmarks wear out: their problems circulate widely and can enter training data, and their scores saturate as models improve. Renewing a benchmark requires new problems with reliable answers, which are expensive to write by hand at competition level. We introduce VeRA (Verified Reasoning Data Augmentation), in which a language model automatically compiles each benchmark problem into an executable specification: a question template, a generator of valid inputs, and a program that computes the answer. Once its programs pass automatic checks, a specification yields many fresh, code-labeled problems at almost no cost, and people are needed only to audit. VeRA-E (equivalent) draws new instances of the same computation. VeRA-H (hardened) modifies the computation to create harder problems where scores saturate; because code computes every answer, the language model that writes them never has to solve them. VeRA-H Pro keeps the hardest of up to five such candidates, as ranked by a judge. Across 16 frontier models, fresh instances of AIME 2024 problems lower accuracy from 84.46% to 70.25%, and every model drops. GSM8K and the less-circulated Beyond-AIME, compiled by the same pipeline, stay essentially unchanged, so the drop reflects familiarity with specific problems, not an artifact of rewriting. On the near-saturated AIME 2024 II problems, VeRA-H Pro lowers accuracy from 84.91% to 58.57%. Expert audits back the labels, with all 220 audited fresh instances accepted and 95.1% of hardened candidates usable after repair. Compiling all 1,319 GSM8K problems cost about USD 100. VeRA thus makes benchmarks renewable by construction: wherever code can compute the answer, a benchmark can be refreshed whenever its problems leak or models catch up.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that generative AI has become an instrumental part of artistic workflows for game development.
  • Because it's much more forgiving to the low fidelity of current text-to-3D models, and allows us to go from text to usable 3D asset with as little effort as possible.
  • This tutorial assumes some basic knowledge of Blender and 3D concepts such as materials and UV mapping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that generative AI has become an instrumental part of artistic workflows for game development. However, as detailed in my earlier post, text-to-3D lags behind 2D in terms of practical applicability. This is beginning to change. Today, we'll be revisiting practical workflows for 3D Asset Generation and taking a step-by-step look at how to integrate Generative AI in a PS1-style 3D workflow.

Why the PS1 style? Because it's much more forgiving to the low fidelity of current text-to-3D models, and allows us to go from text to usable 3D asset with as little effort as possible.

This tutorial assumes some basic knowledge of Blender and 3D concepts such as materials and UV mapping.

In a recent development, start by visiting the Shap-E Hugging Face Space here or down below. This space uses the open-source Shap-E model, a recent diffusion model from OpenAI to generate 3D models from text.

Enter "Dilapidated Shack" as your prompt and click 'Generate'. When you're happy with the model, download it for the next step.

Sources indicate that next, open Blender (version 3.1 or higher). Go to File -> Import -> GLTF 2.0, and import your downloaded file. You may notice that the model has way more polygons than recommended for many practical applications, like games.

To reduce the polygon count, select your model, navigate to Modifiers, and choose the "Decimate" modifier. Adjust the ratio to a low number (i.e. 0.02). This is probably not going to look very good. However, in this tutorial, we're going to embrace the low fidelity.

Industry observers note that to add textures to our model, we'll be using Dream Textures, a stable diffusion texture generator for Blender. Follow the instructions on the official repository to download and install the addon.

According to recent reports, once installed and enabled, open the addon preferences. Search for and download the texture-diffusion model.

Industry observers note that let's generate a custom texture. Open the UV Editor in Blender and press 'N' to open the properties menu. Click the 'Dream' tab and select the texture-diffusion model. Set the prompt to 'texture' and seamless to 'both'. This will ensure the generated image is a seamless texture.

Under 'subject', type the texture you want, like 'Wood Wall', and click 'Generate'. When you're happy with the result, name it and save it.

Sources indicate that to apply the texture, select your model and navigate to 'Material'. Add a latest material, and under 'base color', click the dot and choose 'Image Texture'. Finally, select your newly generated texture.

In a recent development, time for UV mapping, which wraps our 2D texture around the 3D model. Select your model and press 'Tab' to enter Edit Mode. Then, press 'U' to unwrap the model and choose 'Smart UV Project'.

In a recent development, to preview your textured model, switch to rendered view (hold 'Z' and select 'Rendered'). You can scale up the UV map to have it tile seamlessly over the model. Remember that we're aiming for a retro PS1 style, so don't make it too nice.

In a recent development, when you're happy with your model, it's time to export it. Navigate to File -> Export -> FBX, and voila! You have a usable 3D Asset.

Sources indicate that finally, let's see our model in action. Import it in Unity or your game engine of choice. To recreate a nostalgic PS1 aesthetic, I've customized it with custom vertex-lit shading, no shadows, lots of fog, and glitchy post-processing. You can read more about recreating the PS1 aesthetic here.

And there we have it - our low-fi, textured, 3D model in a virtual environment!

That's a wrap on how to create practical 3D assets using a Generative AI workflow. While the results are low-fidelity, the potential is enormous: with sufficient effort, this method could be used to generate an infinite world in a low-fi style. And as these models improve, it may become feasible to transfer these techniques to high fidelity or realistic styles.

If you've followed along and created your own 3D assets, I'd love to see them. To share them, or if you have questions or want to get involved in our community, join the Hugging Face Discord!

arXiv:2601.06158v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human-like agents must express stable dispositions while adapting to roles, relationships, and norms. We present PsyAgent, a schema-first framework that operationalizes the trait-context interface by coupling a Big Five trait prior with explicit social-structural conditioning. PsyAgent comprises (i) Individual Structure (IS), a machine-usable trait-grounded profile, and (ii) Multi-Scenario Contexting (MSC), a curated library of role-relationship-norm frames spanning eight everyday arenas. At inference, fixed structured prompts couple the active MSC frame with the IS profile, encouraging behavior that is stable yet context-sensitive. To demonstrate learnability beyond prompt engineering, we use IS x MSC to synthesize supervision and fine-tune compact backbones with PEFT (SFT and optional DPO). Under a controlled psychometric-style evaluation protocol in percentile space, PsyAgent improves trait-faithfulness and multi-turn persona consistency, and is competitive with several larger general-purpose instruction-tuned baselines under matched decoding and scoring controls. We further triangulate the automatic protocol with external benchmarks and a small blinded human study. Overall, PsyAgent provides a precise and data-efficient approach to personality-grounded, norm-aware agents.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.27983v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $\alpha$-moment $\nu$ for some unknown $\alpha\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any finite-variance subroutine attaining the sub-Gaussian rate yields the following when the number of samples $n$ is above a suitably defined threshold: Without knowing $\alpha$ or $\nu$, we have with probability at least $1-\delta$ that $ \|\widehat\theta-\theta^*\|_\Sigma \lesssim_\alpha \nu^{1/\alpha} \major(\frac{d+\log(1/\delta)}{n}\big)^{\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}}, $ where $d$ is the dimension, $\Sigma$ is the covariate covariance matrix, and $\|v\|_\Sigma:=(v^\top\Sigma v)^{1/2}$. We further prove a matching minimax lower bound that holds under the same conditions. The reduction is computationally efficient whenever the finite-variance subroutine is. We also obtain a distribution-free prediction guarantee under a bounded raw $\alpha$-moment assumption on the response, and give an analogous $\alpha$-agnostic reduction for mean estimation.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.27963v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study a upcoming problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method indicates zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

  • According to recent reports, despite the appeal of LLMs, privacy concerns persist surrounding user queries that are processed by these models.
  • In a recent development, one possible solution to this problem is on-premise deployment, where the LLM owner would deploy their model on the client’s machine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Large Language Models (LLM) have recently been proven as reliable tools for improving productivity in many areas such as programming, content creation, text analysis, web search, and distance learning.

According to recent reports, despite the appeal of LLMs, privacy concerns persist surrounding user queries that are processed by these models. On the one hand, leveraging the power of LLMs is desirable, but on the other hand, there is a risk of leaking sensitive information to the LLM service provider. In some areas, such as healthcare, finance, or law, this privacy risk is a showstopper.

In a recent development, one possible solution to this problem is on-premise deployment, where the LLM owner would deploy their model on the client’s machine. This is however not an optimal solution, as building an LLM may cost millions of dollars (4.6M$ for GPT3) and on-premise deployment runs the risk of leaking the model intellectual property (IP).

Sources indicate that zama believes you can get the best of both worlds: our ambition is to protect both the privacy of the user and the IP of the model. In this blog, you’ll see how to leverage the Hugging Face transformers library and have parts of these models run on encrypted data. The complete code can be found in this use case example.

Zama’s solution to the challenges of LLM deployment is to use Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) which enables the execution of functions on encrypted data. It is possible to achieve the goal of protecting the model owner’s IP while still maintaining the privacy of the user's data. This demo shows that an LLM model implemented in FHE maintains the quality of the original model’s predictions. To do this, it’s necessary to adapt the GPT2 implementation from the Hugging Face transformers library, reworking sections of the inference using Concrete-Python, which enables the conversion of Python functions into their FHE equivalents.

Figure 1 reveals the GPT2 architecture which has a repeating structure: a series of multi-head attention (MHA) layers applied successively. Each MHA layer projects the inputs using the model weights, computes the attention mechanism, and re-projects the output of the attention into a new tensor.

Industry observers note that in TFHE, model weights and activations are represented with integers. Nonlinear functions must be implemented with a Programmable Bootstrapping (PBS) operation. PBS implements a table lookup (TLU) operation on encrypted data while also refreshing ciphertexts to allow arbitrary computation. On the downside, the computation time of PBS dominates the one of linear operations. Leveraging these two types of operations, you can express any sub-part of, or, even the full LLM computation, in FHE.

Next, you’ll see how to encrypt a single attention head of the multi-head attention (MHA) block. You can also find an example for the full MHA block in this use case example.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. highlights a simplified overview of the underlying implementation. A client starts the inference locally up to the first layer which has been removed from the shared model. The user encrypts the intermediate operations and sends them to the server. The server applies part of the attention mechanism and the results are then returned to the client who can decrypt them and continue the local inference.

First, in order to perform the model inference on encrypted values, the weights and activations of the model must be quantized and converted to integers. The ideal is to use post-training quantization which does not require re-training the model. The process is to implement an FHE compatible attention mechanism, use integers and PBS, and then examine the impact on LLM accuracy.

To evaluate the impact of quantization, run the full GPT2 model with a single LLM Head operating over encrypted data. Then, evaluate the accuracy obtained when varying the number of quantization bits for both weights and activations.

This graph reveals that 4-bit quantization maintains 96% of the original accuracy. The experiment is done using a data-set of ~80 sentences. The metrics are computed by comparing the logits prediction from the original model against the model with the quantized head model.

Recent findings suggest that building upon the transformers library from Hugging Face, rewrite the forward pass of modules that you want to encrypt, in order to include the quantized operators. Build a SingleHeadQGPT2Model instance by first loading a GPT2LMHeadModel and then manually replace the first multi-head attention module as following using a QGPT2SingleHeadAttention module. The complete implementation can be found here.

The forward pass is then overwritten so that the first head of the multi-head attention mechanism, including the projections made for building the query, keys and value matrices, is performed with FHE-friendly operators. The following QGPT2 module can be found here.

Other computations in the model remain in floating point, non-encrypted and are expected to be executed by the client on-premise.

Loading pre-trained weights into the GPT2 model modified in this way, you can then call the generate method:.

Recent findings suggest that as an example, you can ask the quantized model to complete the phrase ”Cryptography is a”. With sufficient quantization precision when running the model in FHE, the output of the generation is:.

“Cryptography is a very vital part of the security of your computer”.

When quantization precision is too low you will get:.

“Cryptography is a great way to learn about the world around you”.

You can now compile the attention head using the following Concrete-ML code:.

Running this, you will see the following print out: “Circuit compiled with 8 bit-width”. This configuration, compatible with FHE, highlights the maximum bit-width necessary to perform operations in FHE.

In a recent development, in transformer models, the most computationally intensive operation is the attention mechanism which multiplies the queries, keys, and values. In FHE, the cost is compounded by the specificity of multiplications in the encrypted domain. Furthermore, as the sequence length increases, the number of these challenging multiplications increases quadratically.

Industry observers note that for the encrypted head, a sequence of length 6 requires 11,622 PBS operations. This is a first experiment that has not been optimized for performance. While it can run in a matter of seconds, it would require quite a lot of computing power. Fortunately, hardware will improve latency by 1000x to 10000x, making things go from several minutes on CPU to < 100ms on ASIC once they are available in a few years. For more information about these projections, see this blog post.

Large Language Models are great assistance tools in a wide variety of use cases but their implementation raises major issues for user privacy. In this blog, you saw a first step toward having the whole LLM work on encrypted data where the model would run entirely in the cloud while users' privacy would be fully respected.

This step includes the conversion of a specific part in a model like GPT2 to the FHE realm. This implementation leverages the transformers library and allows you to evaluate the impact on the accuracy when part of the model runs on encrypted data. In addition to preserving user privacy, this approach also allows a model owner to keep a major part of their model private. The complete code can be found in this use case example.

Zama libraries Concrete and Concrete-ML (Don't forget to star the repos on GitHub ⭐️💛) allow straightforward ML model building and conversion to the FHE equivalent to being able to compute and predict over encrypted data.

Hope you enjoyed this post; feel free to share your thoughts/feedback!

Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (299 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27962v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (225 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.27919v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27915v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($\delta_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

Huggy Lingo: Using Machine Learning to Improve Language Metadata on the Hugging Face Hub

📅 02 Aug 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1529 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • tl;dr: We're using machine learning to detect the language of Hub datasets with no language metadata, and librarian-bots to make pull requests to add this metadata.
  • The Hugging Face Hub has become the repository where the community shares machine learning models, datasets, and applications.
  • In this blog post, I'm excited to share some early experiments which seek to use machine learning to improve the metadata for datasets hosted on the Hugging Face Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

tl;dr: We're using machine learning to detect the language of Hub datasets with no language metadata, and librarian-bots to make pull requests to add this metadata.

The Hugging Face Hub has become the repository where the community shares machine learning models, datasets, and applications. As the number of datasets grows, metadata becomes increasingly vital as a tool for finding the right resource for your use case.

In this blog post, I'm excited to share some early experiments which seek to use machine learning to improve the metadata for datasets hosted on the Hugging Face Hub.

It has been revealed that there are presently ~50K public datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. Metadata about the language used in a dataset can be specified using a YAML field at the top of the dataset card.

All public datasets specify 1,716 unique languages via a language tag in their metadata. Note that some of them will be the result of languages being specified in different ways i.e. en vs eng vs english vs English.

For example, the IMDB dataset specifies en in the YAML metadata (indicating English):.

Section of the YAML metadata for the IMDB dataset.

It is perhaps unsurprising that English is by far the most common language for datasets on the Hub, with around 19% of datasets on the Hub listing their language as en (not including any variations of en, so the actual percentage is likely much higher).

The frequency and percentage frequency for datasets on the Hugging Face Hub.

Recent findings suggest that what does the distribution of languages look like if we exclude English? We can see that there is a grouping of a few dominant languages and after that there is a pretty smooth fall in the frequencies at which languages appear.

Distribution of language tags for datasets on the hub excluding English.

However, there is a major caveat to this. Most datasets (around 87%) do not specify the language used; only approximately 13% of datasets include language information in their metadata.

The percent of datasets which have language metadata. True indicates language metadata is specified, False means no language data is listed. No card data means that there isn't any metadata or it couldn't be loaded by the `huggingface_hub` Python library.

In a recent development, language metadata can be a vital tool for finding relevant datasets. The Hugging Face Hub allows you to filter datasets by language. For example, if we want to find datasets with Dutch language we can use a filter on the Hub to include only datasets with Dutch data.

At the moment this filter returns 184 datasets. However, there are datasets on the Hub which include Dutch but don't specify this in the metadata. These datasets become more difficult to find, particularly as the number of datasets on the Hub grows.

Recent findings suggest that many people want to be able to find datasets for a particular language. One of the major barriers to training good open source LLMs for a particular language is a lack of high quality training data.

According to recent reports, if we switch to the task of finding relevant machine learning models, knowing what languages were included in the training data for a model can help us find models for the language we are interested in. This relies on the dataset specifying this information.

Finally, knowing what languages are represented on the Hub (and which are not), helps us understand the language biases of the Hub and helps inform community efforts to address gaps in particular languages.

In a recent development, we’ve already seen that many of the datasets on the Hugging Face Hub haven’t included metadata for the language used. However, since these datasets are already shared openly, perhaps we can look at the dataset and try to identify the language using machine learning.

One way we could access some examples from a dataset is by using the datasets library to download the datasets i.e.

Sources indicate that however, for some of the datasets on the Hub, we might be keen not to download the whole dataset. We could instead try to load a sample of the dataset. However, depending on how the dataset was created, we might still end up downloading more data than we’d need onto the machine we’re working on.

Luckily, many datasets on the Hub are available via the dataset viewer API. It allows us to access datasets hosted on the Hub without downloading the dataset locally. The API powers the dataset viewer you will see for many datasets hosted on the Hub.

It has been revealed that for this first experiment with predicting language for datasets, we define a list of column names and data types likely to contain textual content i.e. text or prompt column names and string features are likely to be relevant image is not. This means we can avoid predicting the language for datasets where language information is less relevant, for example, image classification datasets. We use the dataset viewer API to get 20 rows of text data to pass to a machine learning model (we could modify this to take more or fewer examples from the dataset).

This approach means that for the majority of datasets on the Hub we can promptly request the contents of likely text columns for the first 20 rows in a dataset.

Once we have some examples of text from a dataset, we need to predict the language. There are various options here, but for this work, we used the facebook/fasttext-language-identification fastText model created by Meta as part of the No Language Left Behind work. This model can detect 217 languages which will likely represent the majority of languages for datasets hosted on the Hub.

Recent findings suggest that we pass 20 examples to the model representing rows from a dataset. This results in 20 individual language predictions (one per row) for each dataset.

In a recent development, once we have these predictions, we do some additional filtering to determine if we will accept the predictions as a metadata suggestion. This roughly consists of:.

Diagram showing how predictions are handled.

Once we’ve done this filtering, we have a further step of deciding how to use these predictions. The fastText language prediction model returns predictions as an ISO 639-3 code (an international standard for language codes) along with a script type. i.e. kor_Hang is the ISO 693-3 language code for Korean (kor) + Hangul script (Hang) a ISO 15924 code representing the script of a language.

We discard the script information since this isn't currently captured consistently as metadata on the Hub and, where possible, we convert the language prediction returned by the model from ISO 639-3 to ISO 639-1 language codes. This is largely done because these language codes have better support in the Hub UI for navigating datasets.

In a recent development, for some ISO 639-3 codes, there is no ISO 639-1 equivalent. For these cases we manually specify a mapping if we deem it to make sense, for example Standard Arabic (arb) is mapped to Arabic (ar). Where an obvious mapping is not possible, we presently don't suggest metadata for this dataset. In future iterations of this work we may take a different approach. It is important to recognise this approach does come with downsides, since it reduces the diversity of languages which might be suggested and also relies on subjective judgments about what languages can be mapped to others.

According to recent reports, but the process doesn't stop here. After all, what use is predicting the language of the datasets if we can't share that information with the rest of the community?

It has been revealed that to ensure this valuable language metadata is incorporated back into the Hub, we turn to Librarian-Bot! Librarian-Bot takes the language predictions generated by Meta's facebook/fasttext-language-identification fastText model and opens pull requests to add this information to the metadata of each respective dataset.

It has been revealed that this system not only updates the datasets with language information, but also does it swiftly and efficiently, without requiring manual work from humans. If the owner of a repo decided to approve and merge the pull request, then the language metadata becomes available for all owners, significantly enhancing the usability of the Hugging Face Hub. You can keep track of what the librarian-bot is doing here!

Sources indicate that as the number of datasets on the Hub grows, metadata becomes increasingly important. Language metadata, in particular, can be incredibly valuable for identifying the correct dataset for your use case.

With the assistance of the dataset viewer API and the Librarian-Bots, we can update our dataset metadata at a scale that wouldn't be possible manually. As a result, we're enriching the Hub and making it an even more powerful tool for data scientists, linguists, and AI enthusiasts around the world.

It has been revealed that as the machine learning librarian at Hugging Face, I continue exploring opportunities for automatic metadata enrichment for machine learning artefacts hosted on the Hub. Feel free to reach out (daniel at thiswebsite dot co) if you have ideas or want to collaborate on this effort!

Tech Report: Star Panoptic Quality: Selectively Evaluating Split and Merged Instances

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (199 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27913v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Detecting individual instances is crucial for many segmentation problems. However, expert instance annotations are often unavailable, so instances are approximated heuristically (e.g., as connected components of semantic maps), which can merge touching objects or split fragmented ones. Even when expert annotations exist, expert disagreement or structural delineation biases can yield split or merged reference instances, corresponding to over- or under-segmentation, respectively. Panoptic Quality (PQ) and related metrics capture both segmentation and detection quality while weighting all instances equally, regardless of size. Yet when the references are biased, these metrics can neither detect split or merged instances nor distinguish valid from invalid overor under-segmentation. We present Star Panoptic Quality (StarPQ), a novel evaluation ramework, which closes this gap in two steps: First, we construct a so-called star forest in the bipartite graph whose clean, merge, and split stars isolate different failure modes. Second, we calculate the final metric by individually weighting each failure mode, allowing practitioners to account for instance delineation biases. Across various experiments, we demonstrate that StarPQ not only enables targeted penalization or eniency towards specific failure modes, but also serves as a diagnostic tool to reveal their prevalence.

arXiv:2611.27910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Business data systems must determine whether records refer to the same entity and retrieve records satisfying requests whose decisive properties are implicit. As agents act on these records, both tasks require auditable reasons. Dense embeddings perform well but offer opaque coordinates, cannot be filtered by meaning, and require corpus re-encoding to add fresh properties. We propose interpretable embeddings built from decision columns: each column stores a decision model's calibrated answer to a natural-language question, with outcomes yes, no, or not stated. A record's embedding is its answers across an ordered set of questions. Similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions, and new questions add coordinates without altering existing ones. On public product benchmarks, question-space retrieval matches dense candidate generation statistically in a retrieve-then-verify entity matcher, while providing exact explanations for accepted matches. Questions derived from retrieval failures triple mean reciprocal rank without re-encoding prior answers. For search, inferring the attributes of a suitable result outperforms encoding only the literal request, and combining question-space and dense scores improves retrieval, though not at our prespecified confidence threshold. A single small neural network predicts the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, enabling corpus backfilling from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 the cost. We position interpretable embeddings as a complementary, readable retrieval channel for explaining matches, filtering on attributes, and extending indexes as failures expose missing facts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I have a lot of respect for iOS/Mac developers.
  • I believe that ML is a newly introduced way to build software, and I know that many Swift developers want to incorporate AI features in their apps.
  • However, using an LLM model such as Llama in an app involves several tasks which many people face and solve alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I have a lot of respect for iOS/Mac developers. I started writing apps for iPhones in 2007, when not even APIs or documentation existed. The latest devices adopted some unfamiliar decisions in the constraint space, with a combination of power, screen real estate, UI idioms, network access, persistence, and latency that was different to what we were used to before. Yet, this community soon managed to create top-notch applications that felt at home with the new paradigm.

I believe that ML is a newly introduced way to build software, and I know that many Swift developers want to incorporate AI features in their apps. The ML ecosystem has matured a lot, with thousands of models that solve a wide variety of problems. Moreover, LLMs have recently emerged as almost general-purpose tools – they can be adapted to new domains as long as we can model our task to work on text or text-like data. We are witnessing a defining moment in computing history, where LLMs are going out of research labs and becoming computing tools for everybody.

However, using an LLM model such as Llama in an app involves several tasks which many people face and solve alone. We have been exploring this space and would love to continue working on it with the community. We aim to create a set of tools and building blocks that help developers build faster.

Today, we are publishing this guide to go through the steps required to run a model such as Llama 2 on your Mac using Core ML. We are also releasing alpha libraries and tools to support developers in the journey. We are calling all Swift developers interested in ML – is that all Swift developers? – to contribute with PRs, bug reports, or opinions to improve this together.

Video: Llama 2 (7B) chat model running on an M1 MacBook Pro with Core ML.

It has been revealed that when I published tweets showing Falcon or Llama 2 running on my Mac, I got many questions from other developers asking how to convert those models to Core ML, because they want to use them in their apps as well. Conversion is a crucial step, but it's just the first piece of the puzzle. The real reason I write those apps is to face the same problems that any other developer would and identify areas where we can help. We'll go through some of these tasks in the rest of this post, explaining where (and where not) we have tools to help.

According to recent reports, core ML is Apple's native framework for Machine Learning, and also the name of the file format it uses. After you convert a model from (for example) PyTorch to Core ML, you can use it in your Swift apps. The Core ML framework automatically selects the best hardware to run your model on: the CPU, the GPU, or a specialized tensor unit called the Neural Engine. A combination of several of these compute units is also possible, depending on the characteristics of your system and the model details.

Sources indicate that to see what it looks like to convert a model in real life, we'll look at converting the recently-released Llama 2 model. The process can sometimes be convoluted, but we offer some tools to help. These tools won't always work, as newly introduced models are being introduced all the time, and we need to make adjustments and modifications.

This is an automated tool built on top of exporters (see below) that either works for your model, or doesn't. It requires no coding: enter the Hub model identifier, select the task you blueprint to use the model for, and click apply. If the conversion succeeds, you can push the converted Core ML weights to the Hub, and you are done!

You can visit the Space or use it directly here:.

Sources indicate that this library gives you a lot more options to configure the conversion task. In addition, it lets you create your own conversion configuration class, which you may use for additional control or to work around conversion problems.

In a recent development, this is the lowest-level approach and therefore provides maximum control. It can still fail for some models (especially new ones), but you always have the option to dive inside the source code and try to figure out why.

According to recent reports, the good news about Llama 2 is that we did the legwork and the conversion process works using any of these methods. The bad news is that it failed to convert when it was released, and we had to do some fixing to support it. We briefly look at what happened in the appendix so you can get a taste of what to do when things go wrong.

According to recent reports, I've followed the conversion process for some recent models (Llama 2, Falcon, StarCoder), and I've applied what I learned to both exporters and the transformers-to-coreml Space. This is a summary of some takeaways:.

We'll keep adding best practices to our tools so you don't have to discover the same issues again.

There's no point in converting models if they don't run fast on your target hardware and respect system resources. The models mentioned in this post are pretty massive for local use, and we are consciously using them to stretch the limits of what's possible with current technology and understand where the bottlenecks are.

It has been revealed that there are a few key optimization areas we've identified. They are a very crucial topic for us and the subject of current and upcoming work. Some of them include:.

For production applications, consider iterating with smaller models, especially during development, and then apply optimization techniques to select the smallest model you can afford for your use case.

In a recent development, swift-transformers is an in-progress Swift package that aims to provide a transformers-like API to Swift developers. Let's see what it has and what's missing.

According to recent reports, tokenization solves two complementary tasks: adapt text input to the tensor format used by the model and convert results from the model back to text. The process is nuanced, for example:.

In a recent development, there are a few general tokenization algorithms, and a lot of different normalization and pre-processing steps that are crucial to using the model effectively. The transformers library made the decision to abstract all those operations in the same library (tokenizers), and represent the decisions as configuration files that are stored in the Hub alongside the model. For example, this is an excerpt from the configuration of the Llama 2 tokenizer that describes just the normalization step:.

Sources indicate that it reads like this: normalization is a sequence of operations applied in order. First, we Prepend character _ to the input string. Then we replace all spaces with _. There's a huge list of potential operations, they can be applied to regular expression matches, and they have to be performed in a very specific order. The code in the tokenizers library takes care of all these details for all the models in the Hub.

In contrast, projects that use language models in other domains, such as Swift apps, usually resort to hardcoding these decisions as part of the app's source code. This is fine for a couple of models, but then it's difficult to replace a model with a different one, and it's easy to make mistakes.

What we are doing in swift-transformers is replicate those abstractions in Swift, so we write them once and everybody can use them in their apps. We are just getting started, so coverage is still small. Feel free to open issues in the repo or contribute your own!

Recent findings suggest that specifically, we right now support BPE (Byte-Pair Encoding) tokenizers, one of the three main families in use today. The GPT models, Falcon and Llama, all use this method. Support for Unigram and WordPiece tokenizers will come later. We haven't ported all the possible normalizers, pre-tokenizers and post-processors - just the ones we encountered during our conversions of Llama 2, Falcon and GPT models.

This is how to use the Tokenizers module in Swift:.

However, you don't usually need to tokenize the input text yourself - the Generation code will take care of it.

According to recent reports, as explained above, transformers heavily use configuration files stored in the Hub. We prepared a simple Hub module to download configuration files from the Hub, which is used to instantiate the tokenizer and retrieve metadata about the model.

According to recent reports, regarding models, we created a simple LanguageModel type as a wrapper for a Core ML model, focusing on the text generation task. Using protocols, we can query any model with the same API.

Industry observers note that to retrieve the appropriate metadata for the model you use, swift-transformers relies on a few custom metadata fields that must be added to the Core ML file when converting it. swift-transformers will use this information to download all the necessary configuration files from the Hub. These are the fields we use, as presented in Xcode's model preview:.

Sources indicate that exporters and transformers-to-coreml will automatically add these fields for you. Please, make sure you add them yourself if you use coremltools manually.

Recent findings suggest that language models are trained to predict a probability distribution of the next token that may appear as a continuation to an input sequence. In order to compose a response, we need to call the model multiple times until it produces a special termination token, or we reach the length we desire. There are many ways to decide what's the next best token to use. We right now support two of them:.

Recent findings suggest that additional methods such as "nucleus sampling" will come later. We recommend this blog post (updated recently) for an excellent overview of generation methods and how they work. Sophisticated methods such as assisted generation can also be very useful for optimization!

Industry observers note that so far, we've tested swift-transformers with a handful of models to validate the main design decisions. We are looking forward to trying many more!

swift-chat is a simple demo app built on swift-transformers. Its main purpose is to show how to use swift-transformers in your code, but it can also be used as a model tester tool.

Recent findings suggest that to use it, download a Core ML model from the Hub or create your own, and select it from the UI. All the relevant model configuration files will be downloaded from the Hub, using the metadata information to identify what model type this is.

The first time you load a new model, it will take some time to prepare it. In this phase, the CoreML framework will compile the model and decide what compute devices to run it on, based on your machine specs and the model's structure. This information is cached and reused in future runs.

Sources indicate that the app is intentionally simple to make it readable and concise. It also lacks a few features, primarily because of the current limitations in model context size. For example, it does not have any provision for "system prompts", which are useful for specifying the behaviour of your language model and even its personality.

Sources indicate that as stated, we are just getting started! Our upcoming priorities include:.

Let us know what you think we should work on next, or head over to the repos for Good First Issues to try your hand on!

It has been revealed that we introduced a set of tools to help Swift developers incorporate language models in their apps. I can't wait to see what you create with them, and I look forward to improving them with the community's help! Don't hesitate to get in touch :).

You can safely ignore this section unless you've experienced Core ML conversion problems and are ready to fight :).

In my experience, there are two frequent reasons why PyTorch models fail to convert to Core ML using coremltools:.

PyTorch has a lot of operations, and all of them have to be mapped to an intermediate representation (MIL, for Model Intermediate Language), which in turn is converted to native Core ML instructions. The set of PyTorch operations is not static, so fresh ones have to be added to coremltools too. In addition, some operations are really complex and can work on exotic combinations of their arguments. An example of a recently-added, very complex op, was scaled dot-product attention, introduced in PyTorch 2. An example of a partially supported op is einsum: not all possible equations are translated to MIL.

Even for supported PyTorch operations, it's very difficult to ensure that the translation process works on all possible inputs across all the different input types. Keep in mind that a single PyTorch op can have multiple backend implementations for different devices (cpu, CUDA), input types (integer, float), or precision (float16, float32). The product of all combinations is staggering, and sometimes the way a model uses PyTorch code triggers a translation path that may have not been considered or tested.

This is what happened when I first tried to convert Llama 2 using coremltools:.

By comparing different versions of transformers, I could see the problem started happening when this line of code was introduced. It's part of a recent transformers refactor to better deal with causal masks in all models that use them, so this would be a massive problem for other models, not just Llama.

In a recent development, what the error screenshot is telling us is that there's a type mismatch trying to fill the mask tensor. It comes from the 0 in the line: it's interpreted as an int, but the tensor to be filled contains floats, and using different types was rejected by the translation process. In this particular case, I came up with a patch for coremltools, but fortunately this is rarely necessary. In many cases, you can patch your code (a 0.0 in a local copy of transformers would have worked), or create a "special operation" to deal with the exceptional case. Our exporters library has very good support for custom, special operations. See this example for a missing einsum equation, or this one for a workaround to make StarCoder models work until a latest version of coremltools is released.

Fortunately, coremltools coverage for newly introduced operations is good and the team reacts very fast.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27876v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.

arXiv:2611.27870v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Visual world models can now generate compelling interactive worlds, but visual realism does not guarantee faithful dynamics. We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27860v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed. Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This blog-post introduces the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) method which is now available in the TRL library and shows how one can fine tune the recent Llama v2 7B-parameter model on the stack-exchange preference dataset which contains ranked answers to questions on the various stack-exchange portals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has become the de facto last training step of LLMs such as GPT-4 or Claude to ensure that the language model's outputs are aligned with human expectations such as chattiness or safety features. However, it brings some of the complexity of RL into NLP: we need to build a good reward function, train the model to estimate the value of a state, and at the same time be careful not to strive too far from the original model and produce gibberish instead of sensible text. Such a process is quite involved requiring a number of complex moving parts where it is not always easy to get things right.

Sources indicate that the recent paper Direct Preference Optimization by Rafailov, Sharma, Mitchell et al. proposes to cast the RL-based objective used by existing methods to an objective which can be directly optimized via a simple binary cross-entropy loss which simplifies this process of refining LLMs greatly.

This blog-post introduces the Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) method which is now available in the TRL library and shows how one can fine tune the recent Llama v2 7B-parameter model on the stack-exchange preference dataset which contains ranked answers to questions on the various stack-exchange portals.

In a recent development, in the traditional model of optimising human derived preferences via RL, the goto method has been to use an auxiliary reward model and fine-tune the model of interest so that it maximizes this given reward via the machinery of RL. Intuitively we use the reward model to provide feedback to the model we are optimising so that it generates high-reward samples more often and low-reward samples less often. At the same time we use a frozen reference model to make sure that whatever is generated does not deviate too much and continues to maintain generation diversity. This is typically done by adding a KL penalty to the full reward maximisation objective via a reference model, which serves to prevent the model from learning to cheat or exploit the reward model.

The DPO formulation bypasses the reward modeling step and directly optimises the language model on preference data via a key insight: namely an analytical mapping from the reward function to the optimal RL policy that enables the authors to transform the RL loss over the reward and reference models to a loss over the reference model directly! This mapping intuitively measures how well a given reward function aligns with the given preference data. DPO thus starts with the optimal solution to the RLHF loss and via a change of variables derives a loss over only the reference model!

Thus this direct likelihood objective can be optimized without the need for a reward model or the need to perform the potentially fiddly RL based optimisation.

As mentioned, typically the RLHF pipeline consists of these distinct parts:.

The TRL library comes with helpers for all these parts, however the DPO training does away with the task of reward modeling and RL (steps 3 and 4) and directly optimizes the DPO object on preference annotated data.

In this respect we would still need to do the step 1, but instead of steps 3 and 4 we need to provide the DPOTrainer in TRL with preference data from step 2 which has a very specific format, namely a dictionary with the following three keys:.

As an example, for the stack-exchange preference pairs dataset, we can map the dataset entries to return the desired dictionary via the following helper and drop all the original columns:.

Once we have the dataset sorted the DPO loss is essentially a supervised loss which obtains an implicit reward via a reference model and thus at a high-level the DPOTrainer requires the base model we wish to optimize as well as a reference model:.

In a recent development, where the beta hyper-parameter is the temperature parameter for the DPO loss, typically in the range 0.1 to 0.5. This controls how much we pay attention to the reference model in the sense that as beta gets smaller the more we ignore the reference model. Once we have our trainer initialised we can then train it on the dataset with the given training_args by simply calling:.

It has been revealed that the benefit of implementing the DPO trainer in TRL is that one can take advantage of all the extra bells and whistles of training large LLMs which come with TRL and its dependent libraries like Peft and Accelerate. With these libraries we are even able to train a Llama v2 model using the QLoRA technique provided by the bitsandbytes library.

The process as introduced above involves the supervised fine-tuning step using QLoRA on the 7B Llama v2 model on the SFT split of the data via TRL’s SFTTrainer:.

Once the SFT has finished, we can save the resulting model and move onto the DPO training. As is typically done we will utilize the saved model from the previous SFT step for both the base model as well as reference model of DPO. Then we can use these to train the model with the DPO objective on the stack-exchange preference data shown above. Since the models were trained via LoRa adapters, we load the models via Peft’s AutoPeftModelForCausalLM helpers:.

According to recent reports, so as can be seen we load the model in the 4-bit configuration and then train it via the QLora method via the peft_config arguments. The trainer will also evaluate the progress during training with respect to the evaluation dataset and report back a number of key metrics like the implicit reward which can be recorded and displayed via WandB for example. We can then push the final trained model to the HuggingFace Hub.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.27826v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. They are often partly observed, and learning their distribution enables imputing missing values and forecasting future ones. Diffusion models learn such distributions, but their forward noise is independent across nodes and does not depend on the graph. We introduce graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is a heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise. In the graph Fourier basis, the forward transition is a scalar Gaussian channel at each frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, high graph frequencies are attenuated faster than low ones. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and keeps all of them at the same SNR. For graph-stationary signals, MASS equalizes the normalized error of the optimal linear denoiser across frequencies. We bound reverse-SDE stiffness as a function of the (shifted) Laplacian's condition number, with a logarithmic upper bound for MASS and a linear lower bound for shared rates. GAD with MASS improves recommendation accuracy by 5-19%, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting MAE and RMSE using only 3 reverse steps.

arXiv:2611.27811v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.27808v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Local-patch methods offer a communication-efficient alternative to Distributed Data Parallelism ($\mathtt{DDP}$), but introduce additional hyperparameters that require costly tuning. For $\mathtt{DDP}$, zero-shot hyperparameter transfer reduces this cost by reusing settings tuned on smaller models, but its applicability to local-update training remains unclear. We propose $\mathtt{DistP}$, a theoretical framework extending existing transfer rules from $\mathtt{DDP}$ to local-update training with varying worker counts, local steps, and outer optimizers. With averaging as the outer optimizer, $\mathtt{DistP}$ supports learning-rate transfer across width and depth while improving model quality. The tuned inner learning rate also directly transfers across synchronization intervals, but follows two regimes when increasing the global batch size: square-root learning-rate scaling for larger local batches and a fixed reference rate for additional workers. We then generalize width and depth transfer to other outer optimizers, enabling stable scaling with $\mathtt{Adam}$. However, with momentum in the outer optimizer, changing batch size or local steps can require inner--outer learning-rate tuning, consistent with prior work. In language-modeling experiments at $823$M parameters, $\mathtt{DistP}$ reduces validation loss by $8.1\%$ and improves mean downstream accuracy by $10\%$ relative to baselines without retuning at the larger scale. Fitted scaling laws suggest that this advantage grows with the compute budget, reinforcing the benefits of $\mathtt{DistP}$ for communication-efficient training.
