Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27462v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) imposes detailed obligations on providers of high-risk AI systems but offers limited operational guidance, particularly when these systems integrate third-party General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models. This paper introduces a toolkit that fosters the development of legal-by-design AI-assisted recruitment systems by translating the core legal obligations of the AI Act's conformity assessment---specifically Articles 9--15 and Annex IV---into techno-normative requirements and corresponding guiding questions. While recruitment pipelines may involve components with varying technical complexity and differing levels of algorithmic transparency, this paper focuses on the most challenging case: the integration of third-party GPAI models into critical stages of the selection process, including resume and job description parsing, applicant scoring, and shortlist generation. This scenario presents significant challenges for downstream providers of high-risk AI systems, as it underscores the difficulties in obtaining the technical information needed to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act's techno-normative requirements, both prior to and during market deployment. After introducing the toolkit and illustrating its application through a simplified example, the paper explores informational dependencies between upstream and downstream GPAI model providers. These dependencies may produce informational gaps across the AI supply chain, potentially hindering the collection of evidence necessary for the AI system provider to ensure legal compliance. The resulting lack of technical transparency negatively affects the deployer, who may struggle to maintain meaningful oversight of the system, and ultimately impacts the persons subject to the AI output.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.27447v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Simulation is central to intelligent-vehicle validation, but visual realism or output agreement between a real scene and its synthetic counterpart does not prove that a perception system used the same evidence in both domains. This paper addresses that mechanism-parity gap for paired real-synthetic autonomous-driving perception. It unifies Decisive-Feature Fidelity, which compares decisive evidence maps in a frozen system under test (SUT), with Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity, which projects decisive evidence into semantic scene concepts for diagnosis. The framework is a validation diagnostic rather than a standalone safety certificate: it asks whether output-consistent simulation also preserves the mechanism by which the perception model reaches that output. The empirical evidence comprises ten retrained diffusion ControlNet generators evaluated on a deterministic exact-geometry KITTI-Virtual KITTI 2 subset. Generated counterparts use a 1248-by-376-pixel padded inference canvas and are cropped back to the exact KITTI dimensions before evaluation. The final benchmark reports target-image, output-consistency, and mechanism metrics recomputed from a single audited output set, then adds metric-disagreement cases, bootstrap uncertainty, threshold sensitivity, and concept/cache integrity audits. Across the benchmark, output and appearance fidelity are at most weakly and inconsistently rank-correlated with decisive-mechanism distance for all three frozen SUTs, and a constructed positive control shows the estimator detects a known planted mechanism that output agreement misses, supporting decisive-evidence diagnostics for intelligent-vehicle simulation validation. All numerical claims are restricted to the declared exact-geometry benchmark, ten generators, and three frozen SUTs.

This article is a cross-post from an originally published post on September 2023 on AWS's website.

Consumer engagement and rewards firm Fetch offers an application that lets users earn rewards on their purchases by scanning their receipts. The company also parses these receipts to generate insights into consumer behavior and provides those insights to brand partners. As weekly scans rapidly grew, Fetch needed to improve its speed and precision.

On Amazon Web Services (AWS), Fetch optimized its machine learning (ML) pipeline using Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker , a service for building, training, and deploying ML models with fully managed infrastructure, tools, and workflows. Now, the Fetch app can process scans faster and with significantly higher accuracy.

Using the Fetch app, customers can scan receipts, receive points, and redeem those points for gift cards. To reward consumers for receipt scans instantaneously, Fetch needed to be able to capture text from a receipt, extract the pertinent data, and structure it so that the rest of its system can process and analyze it. With over 80 million receipts processed per week—hundreds of receipts per second at peak traffic—it needed to perform this process rapidly, accurately, and at scale.

In 2021, Fetch set out to optimize its app’s scanning functionality. Fetch is an AWS-native company, and its ML operations team was already using Amazon SageMaker for many of its models. This made the decision to enhance its ML pipeline by migrating its models to Amazon SageMaker a straightforward one.

Throughout the project, Fetch had weekly calls with the AWS team and received support from a subject matter expert whom AWS paired with Fetch. The manufacturer built, trained, and deployed more than five ML models using Amazon SageMaker in 12 months. In late 2022, Fetch rolled out its updated mobile app and new ML pipeline.

Sam Corzine, Machine Learning Engineer, Fetch.

Sam Corzine, Machine Learning Engineer, Fetch.

Sources indicate that fetch’s ML pipeline is powered by several Amazon SageMaker features, particularly Amazon SageMaker Model Training, which reduces the time and cost to train and tune ML models at scale, and Amazon SageMaker Processing, a simplified, managed experience to run data-processing workloads. The firm runs its custom ML models using multi-GPU instances for fast performance. “The GPU instances on Amazon SageMaker are simple to use,” states Ellen Light, backend engineer at Fetch. Fetch trains these models to identify and extract key information on receipts that the company can use to generate valuable insights and reward users. And on Amazon SageMaker, Fetch’s custom ML system is seamlessly scalable. “By using Amazon SageMaker, we have a simple way to scale up our systems, especially for inference and runtime,” says Sam Corzine, ML engineer at Fetch. Meanwhile, standardized model deployments mean less manual work.

In a recent development, fetch heavily relied on the ML training features of Amazon SageMaker, particularly its training jobs, as it refined and iterated on its models. Fetch can also train ML models in parallel, which speeds up development and deployments. “There’s little friction for us to deploy models,” claims Alec Stashevsky, applied scientist at Fetch. “Basically, we don’t have to think about it.” This has increased confidence and improved productivity for the entire manufacturer. In one example, a fresh intern was able to deploy a model himself by his third day on the job.

Industry observers note that since adopting Amazon SageMaker for ML tuning, training, and retraining, Fetch has enhanced the accuracy of its document-understanding model by 200 percent. It continues to fine-tune its models for further improvement. “Amazon SageMaker has been a key tool in building these outstanding models,” says Quency Yu, ML engineer at Fetch. To optimize the tuning process, Fetch relies on Amazon SageMaker Inference Recommender, a capability of Amazon SageMaker that reduces the time required to get ML models in production by automating load testing and model tuning.

It has been revealed that in addition to its custom ML models, Fetch uses AWS Deep Learning Containers (AWS DL Containers), which businesses can use to promptly deploy deep learning environments with optimized, prepackaged container images. This simplifies the process of using libraries from Hugging Face Inc.(Hugging Face), an artificial intelligence technology manufacturer and AWS Partner. Specifically, Fetch uses the Amazon SageMaker Hugging Face Inference Toolkit, an open-source library for serving transformers models, and the Hugging Face AWS Deep Learning Container for training and inference. “Using the flexibility of the Hugging Face AWS Deep Learning Container, we could improve the quality of our models,” claims Corzine. “And Hugging Face’s partnership with AWS meant that it was simple to deploy these models.”.

For every metric that Fetch measures, performance has improved since adopting Amazon SageMaker. The firm has reduced latency for its slowest scans by 50 percent. “Our improved accuracy also creates confidence in our data among partners,” says Corzine. With more confidence, partners will increase their use of Fetch’s solution. “Being able to meaningfully improve accuracy on literally every data point using Amazon SageMaker is a huge benefit and propagates throughout our entire business,” says Corzine.

Recent findings suggest that fetch can now extract more types of data from a receipt, and it has the flexibility to structure resulting insights according to the specific needs of brand partners. “Leaning into ML has unlocked the ability to extract exactly what our partners want from a receipt,” states Corzine. “Partners can make new types of offers because of our investment in ML, and that’s a huge additional benefit for them.”.

In a recent development, customers enjoy the updates too; Fetch has grown from 10 million to 18 million monthly active users since it released the new version. “Amazon SageMaker is a game changer for Fetch,” claims Corzine. “We use almost every feature extensively. As new features come out, they are immediately valuable. It’s hard to imagine having done this project without the features of Amazon SageMaker.” For example, Fetch migrated from a custom shadow testing pipeline to Amazon SageMaker shadow testing—which validates the performance of new ML models against production models to prevent outages. Now, shadow testing is more direct because Fetch can directly compare performance with production traffic.

Recent findings suggest that the ML team at Fetch is continually working on fresh models and iterating on existing ones to tune them for better performance. “Another thing we like is being able to keep our technology stack up to date with new features of Amazon SageMaker,” notes Chris Lee, ML developer at Fetch. The company will continue expanding its use of AWS to different ML use cases, such as fraud prevention, across multiple teams.

In a recent development, already one of the biggest consumer engagement software companies, Fetch aims to continue growing. “AWS is a key part of how we strategy to scale, and we’ll lean into the features of Amazon SageMaker to continue improving our accuracy,” notes Corzine.

Fetch is a consumer engagement company that provides insights on consumer purchases to brand partners. It also offers a mobile rewards app that lets users earn rewards on purchases through a receipt-scanning feature.

Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (257 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27443v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.

THRIFTY: Cost-Constrained Reasoning-Data Synthesis for Small Language Models

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (216 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.27436v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for efficient, specialized deployment, and are typically trained on reasoning trajectories distilled from a larger teacher LLM. Generating this synthetic data is a major cost of the pipeline, especially when the teacher is a frontier model. Existing collection methods, however, are largely cost-unaware, or at best spread a fixed sampling budget uniformly across queries. Such allocation ignores the wide variation in problem difficulty and the strategic over- or under-sampling it invites. Thus, we propose THRIFTY, a Thompson-sampling bandit controller that spends a fixed generation-token budget to collect diverse correct reasoning trajectories, casting the task as a bandits-with-knapsacks problem with a novel diversity-aware objective. It tracks each problem's success probability with an online Beta posterior and spends each token where it expects the most fresh distinct correct solutions. Because repeated solutions add progressively less value, THRIFTY adaptively stops resampling saturated problems, concentrates budget on under-covered ones, and retires the unsolvable at the budget's opportunity cost. On math (AIME, MATH-500) and code (LiveCodeBench) benchmarks, THRIFTY gathers up to 22% more diverse correct trajectories per generation token than both the standard uniform-sampling recipe and the strongest adaptive baseline, with the largest gains in the scarce-budget and hard-problem regimes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, today, we're excited to welcome TII's Falcon 180B to HuggingFace!
  • You can find the model on the Hugging Face Hub (base and chat model) and interact with the model on the Falcon Chat Demo Space.
  • In a recent development, in terms of capabilities, Falcon 180B achieves state-of-the-art results across natural language tasks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, today, we're excited to welcome TII's Falcon 180B to HuggingFace! Falcon 180B sets a latest state-of-the-art for open models. It is the largest openly available language model, with 180 billion parameters, and was trained on a massive 3.5 trillion tokens using TII's RefinedWeb dataset. This represents the longest single-epoch pretraining for an open model.

You can find the model on the Hugging Face Hub (base and chat model) and interact with the model on the Falcon Chat Demo Space.

In a recent development, in terms of capabilities, Falcon 180B achieves state-of-the-art results across natural language tasks. It topped the leaderboard for (pre-trained) open-access models (at the time of its release) and rivals proprietary models like PaLM-2. While difficult to rank definitively yet, it is considered on par with PaLM-2 Large, making Falcon 180B one of the most capable LLMs publicly known.

In this blog post, we explore what makes Falcon 180B so good by looking at some evaluation results and show how you can use the model.

Falcon 180B is a model released by TII that follows previous releases in the Falcon family.

Architecture-wise, Falcon 180B is a scaled-up version of Falcon 40B and builds on its innovations such as multiquery attention for improved scalability. We recommend reviewing the initial blog post introducing Falcon to dive into the architecture. Falcon 180B was trained on 3.5 trillion tokens on up to 4096 GPUs simultaneously, using Amazon SageMaker for a total of ~7,000,000 GPU hours. This means Falcon 180B is 2.5 times larger than Llama 2 and was trained with 4x more compute.

The dataset for Falcon 180B consists predominantly of web data from RefinedWeb (~85%). In addition, it has been trained on a mix of curated data such as conversations, technical papers, and a small fraction of code (~3%). This pretraining dataset is substantial enough that even 3.5 trillion tokens constitute less than an epoch.

The released chat model is fine-tuned on chat and instruction datasets with a mix of several large-scale conversational datasets.

Recent findings suggest that ‼️ Commercial use: Falcon 180b can be commercially used but under very restrictive conditions, excluding any "hosting use". We recommend to check the license and consult your legal team if you are interested in using it for commercial purposes.

It has been revealed that falcon 180B was the best openly released LLM at its release, outperforming Llama 2 70B and OpenAI’s GPT-3.5 on MMLU, and is on par with Google's PaLM 2-Large on HellaSwag, LAMBADA, WebQuestions, Winogrande, PIQA, ARC, BoolQ, CB, COPA, RTE, WiC, WSC, ReCoRD. Falcon 180B typically sits somewhere between GPT 3.5 and GPT4 depending on the evaluation benchmark and further finetuning from the community will be very interesting to follow now that it's openly released.

With 68.74 on the Hugging Face Leaderboard at the time of release, Falcon 180B was the highest-scoring openly released pre-trained LLM, surpassing Meta’s Llama 2.*.

In a recent development, the quantized Falcon models preserve similar metrics across benchmarks. The results were similar when evaluating torch.float16, 8bit, and 4bit. See results in the Open LLM Leaderboard.

Falcon 180B is available in the Hugging Face ecosystem, starting with Transformers version 4.33.

You can easily try the Big Falcon Model (180 billion parameters!) in this Space or in the playground embedded below:.

We ran several tests on the hardware needed to run the model for different use cases. Those are not the minimum numbers, but the minimum numbers for the configurations we had access to.

According to recent reports, the base model has no prompt format. Remember that it’s not a conversational model or trained with instructions, so don’t expect it to generate conversational responses—the pretrained model is a great platform for further finetuning, but you probably shouldn’t driectly use it out of the box. The Chat model has a very simple conversation structure.

In a recent development, as you can see, interactions from the user and responses by the model are preceded by User: and Falcon: separators. We concatenate them together to form a prompt containing the conversation's whole history. We can provide a system prompt to tweak the generation style.

Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that T2I-Adapter is an efficient plug-and-play model that provides extra guidance to pre-trained text-to-image models while freezing the original large text-to-image models. T2I-Adapter aligns internal knowledge in T2I models with external control signals. We can train various adapters according to different conditions and achieve rich control and editing effects.

As a contemporaneous work, ControlNet has a similar function and is widely used. However, it can be computationally expensive to run. This is because, during each denoising step of the reverse diffusion process, both the ControlNet and UNet need to be run. In addition, ControlNet emphasizes the importance of copying the UNet encoder as a control model, resulting in a larger parameter number. Thus, the generation is bottlenecked by the size of the ControlNet (the larger, the slower the process becomes).

T2I-Adapters provide a competitive advantage to ControlNets in this matter. T2I-Adapters are smaller in size, and unlike ControlNets, T2I-Adapters are run just once for the entire course of the denoising process.

Recent findings suggest that over the past few weeks, the Diffusers team and the T2I-Adapter authors have been collaborating to bring the support of T2I-Adapters for Stable Diffusion XL (SDXL) in diffusers. In this blog post, we share our findings from training T2I-Adapters on SDXL from scratch, some appealing results, and, of course, the T2I-Adapter checkpoints on various conditionings (sketch, canny, lineart, depth, and openpose)!

Sources indicate that compared to previous versions of T2I-Adapter (SD-1.4/1.5), T2I-Adapter-SDXL still uses the original recipe, driving 2.6B SDXL with a 79M Adapter! T2I-Adapter-SDXL maintains powerful control capabilities while inheriting the high-quality generation of SDXL!

We built our training script on this official example provided by diffusers.

We encourage the community to use our scripts to train custom and powerful T2I-Adapters, striking a competitive trade-off between speed, memory, and quality.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27425v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work indicates that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27423v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.27410v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so people must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.

TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying newly introduced entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot revision semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. SafeCoder vs. Closed-source Code Assistants

📅 11 Sep 2023 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, software developers have designed methodologies, processes, and tools that help them improve code quality and increase productivity.
  • In "How Google Tests Software" (Addison-Wesley, 2012), Google reports that fixing a bug during system tests - the final testing stage - is 1000x more expensive than fixing it at the unit testing stage.
  • Industry observers note that for all the hype surrounding generative AI, code generation seems a promising way to help developers deliver better code fast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, software developers have designed methodologies, processes, and tools that help them improve code quality and increase productivity. For instance, agile, test-driven development, code reviews, and CI/CD are now staples in the software industry.

In "How Google Tests Software" (Addison-Wesley, 2012), Google reports that fixing a bug during system tests - the final testing stage - is 1000x more expensive than fixing it at the unit testing stage. This puts much pressure on developers - the first link in the chain - to write quality code from the get-go.

Industry observers note that for all the hype surrounding generative AI, code generation seems a promising way to help developers deliver better code fast. Indeed, early studies show that managed services like GitHub Copilot or Amazon CodeWhisperer help developers be more productive.

It has been revealed that however, these services rely on closed-source models that can't be customized to your technical culture and processes. Hugging Face released SafeCoder a few weeks ago to fix this. SafeCoder is a code assistant solution built for the enterprise that gives you state-of-the-art models, transparency, customizability, IT flexibility, and privacy.

In this post, we'll compare SafeCoder to closed-source services and highlight the benefits you can expect from our solution.

SafeCoder is right now built on top of the StarCoder models, a family of open-source models designed and trained within the BigCode collaborative project.

StarCoder is a 15.5 billion parameter model trained for code generation in over 80 programming languages. It uses innovative architectural concepts, like Multi-Query Attention (MQA), to improve throughput and reduce latency, a technique also present in the Falcon and adapted for LLaMa 2 models.

StarCoder has an 8192-token context window, helping it take into account more of your code to generate new code. It can also do fill-in-the-middle, i.e., insert within your code, instead of just appending new code at the end.

Lastly, like HuggingChat, SafeCoder will introduce upcoming state-of-the-art models over time, giving you a seamless upgrade path.

Unfortunately, closed-source code assistant services don't share information about the underlying models, their capabilities, and their training data.

Industry observers note that in line with the Chinchilla Scaling Law, SafeCoder is a compute-optimal model trained on 1 trillion (1,000 billion) code tokens. These tokens are extracted from The Stack, a 2.7 terabyte dataset built from permissively licensed open-source repositories. All efforts are made to honor opt-out requests, and we built a tool that lets repository owners check if their code is part of the dataset.

In the spirit of transparency, our research paper discloses the model architecture, the training process, and detailed metrics.

Unfortunately, closed-source services stick to vague information, such as "[the model was trained on] billions of lines of code." To the best of our knowledge, no metrics are available.

The StarCoder models have been specifically designed to be customizable, and we have already built different versions:.

We also shared the fine-tuning code on GitHub.

In a recent development, every firm has its preferred languages and coding guidelines, i.e., how to write inline documentation or unit tests, or do's and don'ts on security and performance. With SafeCoder, we can help you train models that learn the peculiarities of your software engineering process. Our team will help you prepare high-quality datasets and fine-tune StarCoder on your infrastructure. Your data will never be exposed to anyone.

Unfortunately, closed-source services cannot be customized.

SafeCoder relies on Docker containers for fine-tuning and deployment. It's easy to run on-premise or in the cloud on any container management service.

In addition, SafeCoder includes our Optimum hardware acceleration libraries. Whether you work with CPU, GPU, or AI accelerators, Optimum will kick in automatically to help you save time and money on training and inference. Since you control the underlying hardware, you can also tune the cost-performance ratio of your infrastructure to your needs.

Unfortunately, closed-source services are only available as managed services.

Security is always a top concern, all the more when source code is involved. Intellectual property and privacy must be protected at all costs.

Whether you run on-premise or in the cloud, SafeCoder is under your complete administrative control. You can apply and monitor your security checks and maintain strong and consistent compliance across your IT platform.

SafeCoder doesn't spy on any of your data. Your prompts and suggestions are yours and yours only. SafeCoder doesn't call home and send telemetry data to Hugging Face or anyone else. No one but you needs to know how and when you're using SafeCoder. SafeCoder doesn't even require an Internet connection. You can (and should) run it fully air-gapped.

It has been revealed that closed-source services rely on the security of the underlying cloud. Whether this works or not for your compliance posture is your call. For enterprise users, prompts and suggestions are not stored (they are for individual users). However, we regret to point out that GitHub collects "user engagement data" with no possibility to opt-out. AWS does the same by default but lets you opt out.

Industry observers note that we're very excited about the future of SafeCoder, and so are our customers. No one should have to compromise on state-of-the-art code generation, transparency, customization, IT flexibility, security, and privacy. We believe SafeCoder delivers them all, and we'll keep working hard to make it even better.

If you’re interested in SafeCoder for your company, please contact us. Our team will contact you shortly to learn more about your use case and discuss requirements.

Unlike ground-level panoramic tracking, UAV-mounted omnidirectional cameras observe targets across both azimuth and elevation, introducing geometric challenges under equirectangular projection (ERP). To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{PanoUAV-Tracker (PUTrack)}, a geometry-aware tracking framework combining latitude-adaptive search and seam-aware periodic sampling. Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27381v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-video question answering requires retrieving and integrating relevant evidence from videos spanning hours or even days. Recent agentic approaches organize video information into external memories and iteratively retrieve evidence to answer questions. However, effective retrieval and reasoning remain challenging, as agents must determine what information to search for, which memory sources to access, and how to connect evidence across distant temporal intervals. To address these challenges, we propose Video Memory Skill Agent (VMSA), a framework that jointly designs structured video memories and memory skills for long-video understanding. VMSA constructs three complementary memory components. Segment Caption Memory and Entity Event Memory serve as searchable evidence sources, while Entity-Aware Episode Memory provides broad yet detailed video context to guide evidence retrieval and reasoning. To further support effective memory utilization, VMSA induces memory skills from successful agent trajectories, incrementally refining or extending a compact skill library to guide iterative evidence retrieval, reasoning, and verification. Across seven long-video question-answering benchmarks, VMSA achieves the highest accuracy on all three week-long egocentric benchmarks, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 9.4% on Ego-R1 Bench, and the best or competitive performance on four additional benchmarks. Ablation studies further demonstrate the contributions of all three memory components and memory skills, with memory skills also improving temporal evidence localization.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.27368v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.

arXiv:2611.27353v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As the capabilities of large language models keep improving, traditional mechanistic interpretability methods struggle to keep pace. In contrast, trainable introspection methods emerge as a promising alternative; they repurpose the model itself as a self-diagnostic tool, trained to verbalize what it has learned during finetuning in natural language. While training on datasets of finetuned experts achieves encouraging results, it right now lacks robustness and generalization. Building on the data augmentation framework of MiXup, we introduce WaXup, a method that augments the introspection training set through linear interpolation in the weight space. This is motivated by the linear mode connectivity property: weight averaged experts interpolate the behaviors of the initial experts. We evaluate WaXup on three benchmarks: hidden-behavior models, a meta-dataset of real-world NLP tasks and AuditBench, a challenging alignment auditing suite of models adversarially trained to conceal their behaviors. WaXup improves the accuracy of generated descriptions as well as robustness to various distribution shifts. We hope to improve the reliability of trainable introspection methods towards better and safer models.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We aim to give a clear overview of the pros and cons of each quantization scheme supported in transformers to help you decide which one you should go for.
  • Right now, quantizing models are used for two main purposes:.
  • Industry observers note that so far, two integration efforts have been made and are natively supported in transformers : bitsandbytes and auto-gptq.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We aim to give a clear overview of the pros and cons of each quantization scheme supported in transformers to help you decide which one you should go for.

Right now, quantizing models are used for two main purposes:.

Industry observers note that so far, two integration efforts have been made and are natively supported in transformers : bitsandbytes and auto-gptq. Note that some additional quantization schemes are also supported in the 🤗 optimum library, but this is out of scope for this blogpost.

According to recent reports, to learn more about each of the supported schemes, please have a look at one of the resources shared below. Please also have a look at the appropriate sections of the documentation.

Note also that the details shared below are only valid for PyTorch models, this is currently out of scope for Tensorflow and Flax/JAX models.

In this section, we will go over the pros and cons of bitsandbytes and gptq quantization. Note that these are based on the feedback from the community and they can evolve over time as some of these features are in the roadmap of the respective libraries.

easy: bitsandbytes still remains the easiest way to quantize any model as it does not require calibrating the quantized model with input data (also called zero-shot quantization). It is possible to quantize any model out of the box as long as it contains torch.nn.Linear modules. Whenever a upcoming architecture is added in transformers, as long as they can be loaded with accelerate’s device_map=”auto”, users can benefit from bitsandbytes quantization straight out of the box with minimal performance degradation. Quantization is performed on model load, no need to run any post-processing or preparation step.

Sources indicate that cross-modality interoperability: As the only condition to quantize a model is to contain a torch.nn.Linear layer, quantization works out of the box for any modality, making it possible to load models such as Whisper, ViT, Blip2, etc. in 8-bit or 4-bit out of the box.

0 performance degradation when merging adapters: (Read more about adapters and PEFT in this blogpost if you are not familiar with it). If you train adapters on top of the quantized base model, the adapters can be merged on top of of the base model for deployment, with no inference performance degradation. You can also merge the adapters on top of the dequantized model ! This is not supported for GPTQ.

fast for text generation: GPTQ quantized models are fast compared to bitsandbytes quantized models for text generation. We will address the speed comparison in an appropriate section.

Industry observers note that n-bit support: The GPTQ algorithm makes it possible to quantize models up to 2 bits! However, this might come with severe quality degradation. The recommended number of bits is 4, which seems to be a great tradeoff for GPTQ at this time.

In a recent development, easily-serializable: GPTQ models support serialization for any number of bits. Loading models from TheBloke namespace: https://huggingface.co/TheBloke (look for those that end with the -GPTQ suffix) is supported out of the box, as long as you have the required packages installed. Bitsandbytes supports 8-bit serialization but does not support 4-bit serialization as of today.

AMD support: The integration should work out of the box for AMD GPUs!

slower than GPTQ for text generation: bitsandbytes 4-bit models are slow compared to GPTQ when using generate.

Recent findings suggest that 4-bit weights are not serializable: Currently, 4-bit models cannot be serialized. This is a frequent community request, and we believe it should be addressed very soon by the bitsandbytes maintainers as it's in their roadmap!

calibration dataset: The need of a calibration dataset might discourage some users to go for GPTQ. Furthermore, it can take several hours to quantize the model (e.g. 4 GPU hours for a 175B scale model according to the paper - section 2).

It has been revealed that works only for language models (for now): As of today, the API for quantizing a model with auto-GPTQ has been designed to support only language models. It should be possible to quantize non-text (or multimodal) models using the GPTQ algorithm, but the process has not been elaborated in the original paper or in the auto-gptq repository. If the community is excited about this topic this might be considered in the future.

We decided to provide an extensive benchmark for both inference and fine-tuning adapters using bitsandbytes and auto-gptq on different hardware. The inference benchmark should give customers an idea of the speed difference they might get between the different approaches we propose for inference, and the adapter fine-tuning benchmark should give a clear idea to users when it comes to deciding which approach to use when fine-tuning adapters on top of bitsandbytes and GPTQ base models.

From the benchmark, we can see that bitsandbyes and GPTQ are equivalent, with GPTQ being slightly faster for large batch size. Check this link to have more details on these benchmarks.

The following benchmarks measure the generation speed of the model during inference. The benchmarking script can be found here for reproducibility.

From the two benchmarks, we conclude that generation is faster when we use attention caching, as expected. Moreover, GPTQ is, in general, faster than bitsandbytes. For example, with batch_size=4 and use_cache=True, it is twice as fast! Therefore let’s use use_cache for the next benchmarks. Note that use_cache will consume more memory.

According to recent reports, it is not possible to perform pure training on a quantized model. However, you can fine-tune quantized models by leveraging parameter efficient fine tuning methods (PEFT) and train adapters on top of them. The fine-tuning method will rely on a recent method called "Low Rank Adapters" (LoRA): instead of fine-tuning the entire model you just have to fine-tune these adapters and load them properly inside the model. Let's compare the fine-tuning speed!

From the result, we conclude that bitsandbytes is faster than GPTQ for fine-tuning.

According to recent reports, quantization is great for reducing memory consumption. However, it does come with performance degradation. Let's compare the performance using the Open-LLM leaderboard !

In a recent development, from the results above, we conclude that there is less degradation in bigger models. More interestingly, the degradation is minimal!

In a recent development, in this blogpost, we compared bitsandbytes and GPTQ quantization across multiple setups. We saw that bitsandbytes is better suited for fine-tuning while GPTQ is better for generation. From this observation, one way to get better merged models would be to:.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (326 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.27352v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transportation models, whether they simulate traffic or support planning, are only as reliable as the road networks they run on, down to the lanes and turns at each intersection. Practitioners still take such a network from GIS files and supply its junction and movement data by hand, a task that recurs with each newly introduced base year and design alternative, or they generate it from open map data. OpenStreetMap's lane tags give the correct layout for only 13 of the 44 approaches we test; open map data are often incomplete or inaccurate. Satellite and street-level imagery, in contrast, cover all 44 and show their lanes as painted. Vision-language models (VLMs) can read such imagery, but asked directly they lose geometric consistency when the same lane must be matched across a satellite crop, street-level photos taken from different poses and an ID-labelled network. We therefore present PAVE (Perceive, Anchor, Verify, Edit), a harness in which code measures what can be measured, traffic engineering knowledge enters as general rules and checks, and the model makes only the open judgements, each anchored to network IDs so that checks catch answers that contradict a measurement, a second reading or a traffic rule. Scored against human labels at signalised intersections, PAVE raises the share of exactly correct lane layouts from 49-64% with a single request to 86-91% for two VLMs, with most of the gain coming from reading one approach at a time on traced lanes. The same division of work edits a real network to a planning brief: the model names the links and nodes of each part of a facility, and code builds the edit from a design template. Of 18 edits, 16 pass every network check, against none when the model writes its own code, and 2 contain a design or coding error, against 7. An analysis shows where VLMs lose geometric consistency and which check catches each failure.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.27344v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Action-conditioned video world models imagine future observations under candidate robot actions, providing a promising visual tool for robot policy evaluation and interaction simulation. However, existing video world models often optimize global reconstruction errors instead of emphasizing interaction-relevant regions. As a result, they may preserve overall scene appearance but overlook local interaction details, leading to physically implausible outcomes such as hallucinated contact effects and inconsistent robot-object interactions. We introduce MoReWorld, a unified motion-region-guided framework that uses a shared motion region, the part of the environment that moves in response to the robot's actions, to focus dynamics learning and video generation on interaction-relevant regions. The same motion region guides local motion prediction, region-aware supervision, and motion-gated future-feature conditioning. At inference time, the motion region is predicted as a motion probability map from visual history and robot actions, without requiring future observations or ground-truth motion labels. On WorldSimProbe, MoReWorld achieves the highest overall simulator-faithfulness score, with the strongest performance on local consistency, global consistency, and interaction dynamics. These results indicate that motion-region guidance helps the model preserve scene-level consistency while more faithfully predicting action-conditioned interaction dynamics.

arXiv:2611.27339v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The safety of a request to a vision-language model often depends on the image: asking how to serve a dish is harmless for fresh food and harmful for spoiled food. High accuracy on situational safety benchmarks does not tell us whether a model's safety representation encodes both the scene and the user's intent, because a benchmark can often be solved from one modality alone. Studying frozen vision-language safety representations, we audit five public situational benchmarks and find that each admits a unimodal shortcut: images alone predict the labels, and on same-image prompt pairs a probe that never sees the photograph reaches 0.9645 AUROC. We therefore build a controlled evaluation that crosses safe and hazardous scenes with observation and action requests, so that no single-modality rule can exceed 0.500 group-ranking accuracy. On this control, linear probes on intermediate states of Qwen3-VL-8B and SmolVLM2-2.2B reach 0.958 and 0.930, showing that the scene-intent conjunction is linearly decodable; concatenating separately encoded image and text states already recovers most of this signal, so decodability is not evidence of a fusion mechanism. The same probes screen cheaply but generalize poorly to unseen images and other benchmarks. Reliable multimodal safety evaluation therefore needs controls that rule out unimodal shortcuts before accuracy is read as evidence of joint understanding.

📅 13 Sep 2023 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1284 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in this blog post, we will look at how to fine-tune Llama 2 70B using PyTorch FSDP and related best practices.
  • Industry observers note that fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) is a paradigm in which the optimizer states, gradients and parameters are sharded across devices.
  • It has been revealed that number of nodes: 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in this blog post, we will look at how to fine-tune Llama 2 70B using PyTorch FSDP and related best practices. We will be leveraging Hugging Face Transformers, Accelerate and TRL. We will also learn how to use Accelerate with SLURM.

Industry observers note that fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) is a paradigm in which the optimizer states, gradients and parameters are sharded across devices. During the forward pass, each FSDP unit performs an all-gather operation to get the complete weights, computation is performed followed by discarding the shards from other devices. After the forward pass, the loss is computed followed by the backward pass. In the backward pass, each FSDP unit performs an all-gather operation to get the complete weights, with computation performed to get the local gradients. These local gradients are averaged and sharded across the devices via a reduce-scatter operation so that each device can update the parameters of its shard. For more information on what PyTorch FSDP is, please refer to this blog post: Accelerate Large Model Training using PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel.

It has been revealed that number of nodes: 2. Minimum required is 1.Number of GPUs per node: 8GPU type: A100GPU memory: 80GBintra-node connection: NVLinkRAM per node: 1TBCPU cores per node: 96inter-node connection: Elastic Fabric Adapter.

We encountered three main challenges when trying to fine-tune LLaMa 70B with FSDP:.

Industry observers note that FSDP wraps the model after loading the pre-trained model. If each process/rank within a node loads the Llama-70B model, it would require 70*4*8 GB ~ 2TB of CPU RAM, where 4 is the number of bytes per parameter and 8 is the number of GPUs on each node. This would result in the CPU RAM getting out of memory leading to processes being terminated.

Recent findings suggest that saving entire intermediate checkpoints using FULL_STATE_DICT with CPU offloading on rank 0 takes a lot of time and often results in NCCL Timeout errors due to indefinite hanging during broadcasting. However, at the end of training, we want the whole model state dict instead of the sharded state dict which is only compatible with FSDP.

We need to improve the speed and reduce the VRAM usage to train faster and save compute costs.

Let’s look at how to solve the above challenges and fine-tune a 70B model!

Before we get started, here's all the required resources to reproduce our results:.

Codebase: https://github.com/pacman100/DHS-LLM-Workshop/tree/main/chat_assistant/sft/training with flash-attn V2.

FSDP config: https://github.com/pacman100/DHS-LLM-Workshop/blob/main/chat_assistant/training/configs/fsdp_config.yaml.

SLURM script launch.slurm: https://gist.github.com/pacman100/1cb1f17b2f1b3139a63b764263e70b25.

Model: meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-chat-hf.

Dataset: smangrul/code-chat-assistant-v1 (mix of LIMA+GUANACO with proper formatting in a ready-to-train format).

First follow these steps to install Flash Attention V2: Dao-AILab/flash-attention: Fast and memory-efficient exact attention (github.com). Install the latest nightlies of PyTorch with CUDA ≥11.8. Install the remaining requirements as per DHS-LLM-Workshop/code_assistant/training/requirements.txt. Here, we will be installing 🤗 Accelerate and 🤗 Transformers from the main branch.

Recent findings suggest that PRs huggingface/transformers#25107 and huggingface/accelerate#1777 solve the first challenge and requires no code changes from user side. It does the following:.

Below is the output snippet on a 7B model on 2 GPUs measuring the memory consumed and model parameters at various stages. We can observe that during loading the pre-trained model rank 0 & rank 1 have CPU total peak memory of 32744 MB and 1506 MB , respectively. Therefore, only rank 0 is loading the pre-trained model leading to efficient usage of CPU RAM. The whole logs at be found here.

Sources indicate that it is addressed via choosing SHARDED_STATE_DICT state dict type when creating FSDP config. SHARDED_STATE_DICT saves shard per GPU separately which makes it quick to save or resume training from intermediate checkpoint. When FULL_STATE_DICT is used, first process (rank 0) gathers the whole model on CPU and then saving it in a standard format.

Let’s create the accelerate config via below command:.

The resulting config is available here: fsdp_config.yaml. Here, the sharding strategy is FULL_SHARD. We are using TRANSFORMER_BASED_WRAP for auto wrap policy and it uses _no_split_module to find the Transformer block name for nested FSDP auto wrap. We use SHARDED_STATE_DICT to save the intermediate checkpoints and optimizer states in this format recommended by the PyTorch team. Make sure to enable broadcasting module parameters from rank 0 at the start as mentioned in the above paragraph on addressing Challenge 1. We are enabling bf16 mixed precision training.

For final checkpoint being the whole model state dict, below code snippet is used:.

According to recent reports, flash Attention and enabling gradient checkpointing are required for faster training and reducing VRAM usage to enable fine-tuning and save compute costs. The codebase at the moment uses monkey patching and the implementation is at chat_assistant/training/llama_flash_attn_monkey_patch.py.

FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness introduces a way to compute exact attention while being faster and memory-efficient by leveraging the knowledge of the memory hierarchy of the underlying hardware/GPUs - The higher the bandwidth/speed of the memory, the smaller its capacity as it becomes more expensive.

If we follow the blog Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles, we can figure out that Attention module on current hardware is memory-bound/bandwidth-bound. The reason being that Attention mostly consists of elementwise operations as shown below on the left hand side. We can observe that masking, softmax and dropout operations take up the bulk of the time instead of matrix multiplications which consists of the bulk of FLOPs.

This is precisely the problem that Flash Attention addresses. The idea is to remove redundant HBM reads/writes. It does so by keeping everything in SRAM, perform all the intermediate steps and only then write the final result back to HBM, also known as Kernel Fusion. Below is an illustration of how this overcomes the memory-bound bottleneck.

Tiling is used during forward and backward passes to chunk the NxN softmax/scores computation into blocks to overcome the limitation of SRAM memory size. To enable tiling, online softmax algorithm is used. Recomputation is used during backward pass in order to avoid storing the entire NxN softmax/score matrix during forward pass. This greatly reduces the memory consumption.

For a simplified and in depth understanding of Flash Attention, please refer the blog posts ELI5: FlashAttention and Making Deep Learning Go Brrrr From First Principles along with the original paper FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.

According to recent reports, to run the training using Accelerate launcher with SLURM, refer this gist launch.slurm. Below is an equivalent command showcasing how to use Accelerate launcher to run the training. Notice that we are overriding main_process_ip , main_process_port , machine_rank , num_processes and num_machines values of the fsdp_config.yaml. Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.27326v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Chain-of-thought prompting significantly improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) but incurs high inference costs due to lengthy autoregressive decoding. While previous efficiency approaches reduce costs by discarding tokens or utilizing continuous latent representations, these lossy methods fundamentally sacrifice interpretability and auditability. In this work, we introduce a novel compression framework for intermediate reasoning. We apply Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) to reasoning corpora to learn a compressed vocabulary of Private Use Area (PUA) tokens, each representing frequent semantic spans. After expanding the LLM's vocabulary, we fine-tune the model via strictly 1:1, our method is lossless. We evaluate our approach on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-14B, and Qwen2.5-32B across four diverse benchmarks. Our method reduces total generated tokens by 14.7% on average with reasoning trace lengths dropping by up to 27.1%, while incurring a negligible average accuracy cost of 1.6 percentage points. Crucially, this approach is orthogonal to existing lossy methods, allowing practitioners to stack lossless and irreversible compression techniques. We demonstrate that a compressed intermediate language provides a highly efficient computational resource that accelerates inference while fully preserving the transparency of LLM reasoning.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (205 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.27317v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps from language models, it is unclear which words in the context actually steer the CoT. We identify Phantom Context Influence (PCI): language models are disproportionately steered by semantically irrelevant context words, even as the same models deny those words' relevance when asked. To localize PCI, we introduce Leave-One-Out Word JSD analysis, which removes one context word at a time from the otherwise intact context to isolate its marginal effect on the next-token distribution; words whose removal flips the prediction (pivot words) are passed to the same LLM to self-judge whether it recognizes this predictive dependence. Across four models and three benchmarks, language models largely do not know which words steer their reasoning, a mismatch we call the Generation-Judgment Contradiction. Inspired by this phenomenon, we propose Online KV Suppression: it scores every prompt word's influence over the whole chain of thought in a single pass, then zeroes the KV-cache entries of the highest-influence word the model itself judges inert and redecodes. This single-word intervention improves CoT accuracy across four models and five reasoning benchmarks, by up to 8.9 percentage points on math reasoning benchmark.

Introducing Würstchen: Fast Diffusion for Image Generation

📅 13 Sep 2023 | ⏱️ 4 min read (867 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Würstchen is a diffusion model, whose text-conditional component works in a highly compressed latent space of images.
  • Well, this one is pretty fast and efficient.
  • Industry observers note that in addition to that, another greatly significant benefit of Würstchen comes with the reduced training costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Würstchen is a diffusion model, whose text-conditional component works in a highly compressed latent space of images. Why is this key? Compressing data can reduce computational costs for both training and inference by orders of magnitude. Training on 1024×1024 images is way more expensive than training on 32×32. Usually, other works make use of a relatively small compression, in the range of 4x - 8x spatial compression. Würstchen takes this to an extreme. Through its novel design, it achieves a 42x spatial compression! This had never been seen before, because common methods fail to faithfully reconstruct detailed images after 16x spatial compression. Würstchen employs a two-stage compression, what we call Stage A and Stage B. Stage A is a VQGAN, and Stage B is a Diffusion Autoencoder (more details can be found in the  paper). Together Stage A and B are called the Decoder, because they decode the compressed images back into pixel space. A third model, Stage C, is learned in that highly compressed latent space. This training requires fractions of the compute used for current top-performing models, while also allowing cheaper and faster inference. We refer to Stage C as the Prior.

Well, this one is pretty fast and efficient. Würstchen’s biggest benefits come from the fact that it can generate images much faster than models like Stable Diffusion XL, while using a lot less memory! So for all of us who don’t have A100s lying around, this will come in handy. Here is a comparison with SDXL over different batch sizes:.

Industry observers note that in addition to that, another greatly significant benefit of Würstchen comes with the reduced training costs. Würstchen v1, which works at 512x512, required only 9,000 GPU hours of training. Comparing this to the 150,000 GPU hours spent on Stable Diffusion 1.4 suggests that this 16x reduction in cost not only benefits researchers when conducting fresh experiments, but it also opens the door for more organizations to train such models. Würstchen v2 used 24,602 GPU hours. With resolutions going up to 1536, this is still 6x cheaper than SD1.4, which was only trained at 512x512.

You can also find a detailed explanation video here:.

You can either try it using the Demo here:.

Otherwise, the model is available through the Diffusers Library, so you can use the interface you are already familiar with. For example, this is how to run inference using the AutoPipeline:.

Sources indicate that würstchen was trained on image resolutions between 1024x1024 & 1536x1536. We sometimes also observe good outputs at resolutions like 1024x2048. Feel free to try it out. We also observed that the Prior (Stage C) adapts extremely fast to new resolutions. So finetuning it at 2048x2048 should be computationally cheap.

Recent findings suggest that all checkpoints can also be seen on the Huggingface Hub. Multiple checkpoints, as well as future demos and model weights can be found there. Right now there are 3 checkpoints for the Prior available and 1 checkpoint for the Decoder. Take a look at the documentation where the checkpoints are explained and what the different Prior models are and can be used for.

Because Würstchen is fully integrated in diffusers, it automatically comes with various goodies and optimizations out of the box. These include:.

Starting from version 2.0, PyTorch has integrated a highly optimised and resource-friendly version of the attention mechanism called torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention or SDPA. Depending on the nature of the input, this function taps into multiple underlying optimisations. Its performance and memory efficiency outshine the traditional attention model. Remarkably, the SDPA function mirrors the characteristics of the flash attention technique, as highlighted in the research paper Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness penned by Dao and team.

If you're using Diffusers with PyTorch 2.0 or a later version, and the SDPA function is accessible, these enhancements are automatically applied. Get started by setting up torch 2.0 or a newer version using the official guidelines!

For an in-depth look at how diffusers leverages SDPA, check out the documentation.

If you're on a version of Pytorch earlier than 2.0, you can still achieve memory-efficient attention using the xFormers library:.

If you're on the hunt for an extra performance boost, you can make use of torch.compile. It is best to apply it to both the prior's and decoder's main model for the biggest increase in performance.

Industry observers note that bear in mind that the initial inference step will take a long time (up to 2 minutes) while the models are being compiled. After that you can just normally run inference:.

According to recent reports, and the good news is that this compilation is a one-time execution. Post that, you're set to experience faster inferences consistently for the same image resolutions. The initial time investment in compilation is rapidly offset by the subsequent speed benefits. For a deeper dive into torch.compile and its nuances, check out the official documentation.

The ability to train this model was only possible through compute resources provided by Stability AI. We wanna say a special thank you to Stability for giving us the possibility to pursue this kind of research, with the chance to make it accessible to so many more people!

A Framework for AI-Ready Data in Earth and Environmental Science

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (255 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27313v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), specifically machine learning (ML), is increasingly integral to Earth and environmental research, yet the suitability of current research data infrastructures for supporting AI workflows remains poorly defined. While the FAIR principles provide a foundation for scientific data management, they do not explicitly address several requirements arising when datasets are used for training, evaluating, and deploying AI models. This article presents a practically motivated framework for assessing and improving AI-readiness of research data within distributed Earth and environmental data infrastructures. The framework was developed through a structured, community-driven process, beginning with a review of existing literature and readiness frameworks combined with feedback from a limited survey of scientists applying ML methods. Its main aspects were shaped by a multidisciplinary expert group representing data providers, infrastructure developers, data managers, and AI practitioners. It identifies 25 criteria covering data preparation, data quality, documentation, access, and supervised learning targets. The criteria emphasize aspects particularly relevant to AI applications, including provenance, treatment of missing data, bias documentation, uncertainty characterization, machine-actionable metadata, efficient access formats, and the quality and reproducibility of target generation. Application to a broad range of representative environmental use cases highlights how the relevance of individual criteria varies by application. We argue that AI-readiness should be understood primarily as a property of transparency and fitness for purpose rather than as a fixed level of data quality. The framework lays a foundation for communication and community-driven action to advance AI-ready data and support next-generation AI-enabled scientific workflows.

This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs' performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is notable for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.27290v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Latent action models let a robot policy learn from video by turning the change between two frames into a training target. In egocentric video, a cup can move across the image because a hand pushes it or because the wearer turns. Both changes help predict the next frame, but only the first describes manipulation. During training, EgoLAM supervises the action code with measured wrist motion and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model. Even when the wearer turns while pushing a cup, the training target still describes how the hand pushed it. The action encoder pools object slots around each hand, and wrist translation and rotation can be decoded from the code in a common reference frame. Extracting a code then requires only two RGB frames. Alongside LARYBench classification and regression, we measure how much wrist motion a frozen code retains and how strongly it responds to a synthetic view or lighting change. EgoLAM has the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three LIBERO suites, policies pretrained on its codes and fine-tuned on expert demonstrations achieve 79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model in each suite on average.

Preserving Pretrained CFG Structure in RL for Diffusion Models with Conditional Contrast Regularization

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.27288v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important component in the post-training of diffusion models. In practice, however, standard RL often improves the target reward without reliably preserving holistic generation quality, leading to unstable reward-quality trade-offs that we view as a form of reward hacking. Since Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is known to improve visual clarity, prompt alignment, and perceptual quality in generation, we investigate whether its underlying structure can serve as a useful prior during RL. We present a unified geometric view that interprets both CFG and RL as correction vectors in a common prediction space, and identify the projection of the RL-induced correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a useful diagnostic of quality-related structural preservation. Geometric analysis and rotation intervention further show that the pretrained CFG direction carries information useful for generation quality that reward-driven RL updates do not necessarily preserve. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.
